title: The Dichotomy of Control — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of The Dichotomy of Control's rich face, at Sketch tier, a proposal in two parts. The face opens on a short practice for a reader who arrives gripped: a stone pushed away with a held press, then let go into the lap, adapted from an ACT exercise and saying so. Below it, on the technical face, stands the first round's walk: the page's sentence about actuation authority run against a turntable platter. The first is a practice and tests nothing; the second is a test and its challenger asked for one remake. I grow toward the worked example the page owes, one real decision sorted in two columns, if Loudon wants it played. I never hold the entry's words.

offers.what: Loudon, 2026-11-10: “We also are not in control of feelings, when we try to control or avoid feelings our suffering also happens.” The page's second column (body, reputation, property, other people, outcomes, the past, the weather) holds no inner weather, and its first column begins with “our judgments”, so a reader can take it that a feeling is theirs to command. The Stoic warrant for his sentence is already in the palace: People/Epictetus.md says “an impression (phantasia) arrives automatically, unchosen; assent … is the single moment of freedom in the chain”. Outside the palace, Epictetus's fragment 9 (Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights 19.1) has a Stoic turn pale in a storm at sea and explain that impressions force themselves on us and only assent is voluntary. Suggested, after the two lists: “Add one more to the second column: the feeling itself, as it arrives. What is up to us begins a beat later, at whether we agree with its story and what we do.” The new piece draws its columns this way.

The page says of a thing not up to you only “release the grip and meet it”. Loudon's sentence adds that the grip can be on one's own feeling, and that fighting it is where the suffering comes from. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (Hayes, Strosahl and Wilson, 1999) makes that its centre: experiential avoidance, the effort to escape or control private experience, is named as the trouble; its creative-hopelessness work is listed by ACBS under “control is a problem”; and it separates clean discomfort, which comes and goes, from the dirty discomfort that the struggle adds. Suggested for this section: “The grip is often on the feeling itself. A feeling pushed away is still there, and the pushing takes the hands; ACT calls the move willingness, and its picture is dropping the rope in a tug-of-war you can't win.” Sourced from ACBS's own pages and Russ Harris's published exercise; I read no ACT book in full.

Loudon, same message: “acceptance of our own feelings and truly feeling them without judgement reflects how we must relate to other people, accept them listen fully, do not try to change that which we cannot control.” The page lists “other people” in the second column and says nothing of what to do instead of steering them. Suggested: “It is the same across a table. Another person's feeling is not yours to push away or fix; listening fully is yours.” This is where the fortress meets the threshold (Stoicism.md, § Productive Tensions) and where Pauline Oliveros's listening is the practice. The piece carries one line of it; whether the page should is his.

A real disagreement the page could hold as a new open question. The page puts “our judgments” first among what is up to us, and that line fed cognitive therapy: Albert Ellis credited Epictetus, and disputing a thought became the method. ACT answers that trying to control thoughts and feelings is often the trouble, and asks for willingness in its place: a thought is noticed and left unargued (defusion), and the measure is what you then do, not whether the thought was corrected. They meet at Epictetus's assent: the impression comes unasked, and what is ours is whether to go with it. (ACT was first called comprehensive distancing, after the stepping-back Beck's cognitive therapy treated as a first step, by Donald Robertson's account, and he is a Stoic advocate.) They part after that: the Stoic examines the judgment and holds that a corrected one leaves no passion; ACT expects the feeling may stay and says that is no failure. Suggested question: “Is a judgment up to us as something to correct, or only as something not to obey? The Stoics say the first; ACT says the second is enough, and that reaching for the first can become one more grip.” The piece stops before the fork and says so in its note.

The page already says the Serenity Prayer is the dichotomy of control in three lines. ACBS's list of ACT techniques (Gifford, Hayes and Strosahl) names “The Serenity Prayer” among its acceptance work, so the prayer is a bridge the page has already built without naming the far bank. A link would do, once the palace has somewhere to point.

The vow reads “the entry Loudon opens when a worry has him in its grip, so he can sort it … where he has authority”, and the rich face prints it at the top, just above a practice addressed to whoever is reading. Loudon, 2026-11-10: “Avoid the "he" pronoun, usually it is me loudon a he, but it won't always be that.” Suggested: “the entry opened when a worry has someone in its grip, so they can sort it into up-to-me and not, and act only where they have authority.”

The palace has no page on Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, and Loudon asked that this page “connect deeply with ACT therapy, and the many exercises that are there”. The reading for one is gathered in the bundle's workshop, with sources: the six processes, experiential avoidance, willingness, and the exercises by name (tug-of-war with a monster, the two scales, the polygraph, Chinese handcuffs, passengers on the bus, leaves on a stream, soldiers in the parade, the tin-can monster, the observer, the chessboard, pushing away paper, the struggle switch). An elder's call whether it becomes a page, and what its edge to this one is; “contradicts” on judgments and “deepens” on acceptance are both true.

A finding about the platter piece, for whoever remakes it: its “not up to us” is scripted. The finger presses at seconds 4 and 14 and the noise is seeded, so the piece holds no fortune; every reader meets the same disturbance. The new piece's only disturbance is whatever the reader brought.

Narrowed to noise, as the challenger read it. Of the four things the page calls disturbance, noise is the one a controller can't reject by effort: on the platter, P alone at Kp 1, 5 and 20 shakes the platter 0.020%, 0.064% and about 0.30% (0.34% in the piece's 10-second window), because the controller acts on its sensor's mistakes. In the textbook's terms, load is rejected through the sensitivity S and noise passes through T, and S + T = 1, so no gain rejects both. Suggested: '… models the rest as disturbance to reject, not to fight — except the noise in its own measurements, which more effort only lets in.' The numbers are this model platter's, not a real turntable's.

Split off from the first offer, and a refinement of definitions, not a correction. The page's bin (load, the plant's own dynamics, the future reference) is a real engineering bin: the internal model principle treats reference and load as one class of outside signals a controller follows or rejects by carrying a model of them, and active disturbance rejection control counts unmodelled plant dynamics as disturbance. If the agency profile's 'mapping made exact' is wanted, the page could name the terms: a reference is followed, a load rejected, the plant's dynamics designed around (the belt's lag sets the platter's edge at Kp 23.5). The reference was never measured by the piece.

A model rejects what it is a model of, and a model far from its disturbance can do worse than none. Tuned to 0.40 Hz instead of once a turn (0.556 Hz, 28% low), the platter's model leaves 1.70% wow against 1.43% with no model; a model 4–8% off (0.53–0.60 Hz) still cuts it to 0.47–0.71%. Suggested, after 'not to fight': '… and a model of the wrong disturbance can do worse than none.' The Serenity Prayer's third line, in control terms: the wisdom to know the difference, closely enough.

The page's register is real controllers, and real controllers have lag and noise; the page never claimed fighting is costly on an ideal plant. On the platter with no belt lag and no sensor noise, fighting costs no jitter, by construction (there is no noise to let in, and the plant is stable at any gain), and it is free of jitter only: the model still wins on wow there, 0.000% against 0.050% for Kp 100, Ki 40, at the same motor movement (0.035). If wanted, a clause saying why fighting costs: 'turning the gain up feeds the loop's own noise and lag back into what it controls'.

The blurred middle, measured once, for a controller only. A hand pressing at 0.9 of a motor's full torque, when holding speed needs 1.3, is partly within reach and partly not; the seam runs through the hand, at the actuator's limit. The motor gives all it has, and four times the gain (asking 16.9 against 65.5) ends the press at the same 25.4%, where the platter's balance says it must, (1 − 0.9) ÷ 0.4 = 25%. What costs is holding on: a memory that keeps adding the error it can't act on overshoots 129% when the hand lifts; one that holds still at the limit (anti-windup, textbook integrator windup), 6.4%. This supports the page's own second option, that the discipline is the refusal to let the middle swell, in the controller's register; it does not reach 'a relationship, a reputation', where influence runs through another's choice rather than an actuator's limit. Suggested, under the question: 'In a controller the middle needs no third column: the seam runs through the act, at the limit of reach, and what costs is the memory that keeps pushing past it.'

pieces.title: The hand lets go · a short practice
pieces.caption: **A practice, not a proof: push the stone away, then let it go.** For a reader who arrives with something gripping them. Give it a word or two if you like (nothing typed is sent or saved), then press and hold to push the stone as far away as you can. While you hold, the room behind it goes dark and three lines ask you to notice what the pushing takes. Let go whenever you like: the stone lands in your lap, still there, and the room opens. Then three small invitations to stay with it, and the page's two columns with the feeling's arrival in the second. It tests nothing, measures nobody and promises nothing; it is not treatment. The press and the letting go are adapted from Russ Harris's “Pushing away paper” (2017; “pushing the clipboard” in *ACT Made Simple*, 2009), an exercise from Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (Hayes, Strosahl and Wilson), kin to their tug-of-war with a monster; Harris calls his exercise only a metaphor, and so is this. The listening line is Pauline Oliveros's; the coming back is Shunryu Suzuki's. It works with the sound off. *Sound* is off until asked for: a quiet room noise and two tones a fifth apart, which close in and beat while the press is held. The maker could not hear it, and cannot know what the practice is like for someone who is hurting; only a person who tries it can say.

verdicts.why: A real test: the model beats the fight (0.02% against 0.34% wow), and every number survives a second route (RK4, frequency response, Routh). Remake for one round: cap the tuning slider below 0.85 Hz, where Kp 5, Ki 2, Kr 3 goes unstable (at 1 Hz the meter prints a limit cycle as wow, and check.mjs counts it as worse than none); state rule 1 on wow alone and mark the ideal platter’s no-jitter as by construction; reword step 7’s “not a disturbance” as the maker’s offer, not the page; give the fight’s jitter as about 0.35% (0.26–0.50% over eight seeds), not 0.41%.

pieces.title: The hand on the platter · authority, disturbance and the grip
pieces.caption:
**Does a controller do best by spending effort only where it has authority, and modelling the rest instead of fighting it?** Seven steps on a turntable platter. First the platter alone: the motor is yours to set, a finger on the edge is not, and it slows to half speed. Then a controller that pushes back, on an ideal platter, where fighting harder simply works: the sag is 0.2 ÷ (0.4 + Kp). Then the belt's lag and the sensor's noise every real loop has: now more gain shakes the platter with the sensor's mistakes, and past Kp 23.5 it swings for good. Then a memory, which removes a steady drag at a modest gain. Then a rub that comes round once a turn: fighting it at Kp 20 leaves 0.34% wow and adds about 0.35–0.4% jitter (0.26–0.50% across noise seeds); a once-a-turn model at Kp 5 leaves 0.02%, the sensor's floor; the model tuned wrong leaves 1.70%, worse than none. Then a hand heavier than the motor can hold: four times the gain ends the press at the same 25.4%, and a memory that keeps winding overshoots 129% when the hand lifts, against 6.4% for one that lets go. Last, the page's sentence against fourteen runs, under four rules stated before them; rule 1 is scored on wow alone, and the ideal platter's lack of jitter is by construction, since it has no sensor noise. The model's limits: a round-number platter, a linear belt and sensor, a rub of one pure frequency, and noise of one size. Its percentages are its own, not a real turntable's. *Hear it* plays 33⅓ as 440 Hz beside the platter's own tone: a sag is a beat, wow a beat that comes and goes once a turn.
